Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3,\,y=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1,\,t\in [\frac{\pi}{5},\frac{47 \pi}{60}].
$$

Give an exact answer.

$L=$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3) \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1) \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\frac{\pi}{5}}^{\frac{47 \pi}{60}}\sqrt{{(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\frac{\pi}{5}}^{\frac{47 \pi}{60}}\sqrt{25{cos}^{2}⁡t+25{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\frac{\pi}{5}}^{\frac{47 \pi}{60}}\sqrt{25({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\frac{\pi}{5}}^{\frac{47 \pi}{60}}\sqrt{25}\,\text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{\frac{\pi}{5}}^{\frac{47 \pi}{60}}\text{d}t \\  & =5t\,{|}_{\frac{\pi}{5}}^{\frac{47 \pi}{60}} \\  & =5(\frac{47 \pi}{60}-\frac{\pi}{5}) \\  & =5(\frac{7 \pi}{12}) \\  & =\frac{35 \pi}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length $L$ of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=4\left(t-\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}\right),\,y=4\left({t}^{2}\right),\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Give an exact answer.

$L=$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\left(t-\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}\right)) \\  & =4\left(1-{t}^{2}\right), \end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\left({t}^{2}\right)) \\  & =4\left(2t\right). \end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{16\left((1-{t}^{2})^{2}+(2t)^{2}\right)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{16\left(1-2{t}^{2}+{t}^{4}+4{t}^{2}\right)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{16\left(1+2{t}^{2}+{t}^{4}\right)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{16\left((1+{t}^{2})^{2}\right)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\left((t+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3})\,\right){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4\left((1+\frac{1}{3})-0\right) \\  & =4\left(\frac{4}{3}\right). \end{aligned}
$$
